title: Hackers Breach Air Force's Flagship Cloud One Platform, Reuters Reports
excerpt: Hackers breached the U.S. Air Force's flagship Cloud One computing platform, Reuters reported Nov. 27, in an intrusion discovered within the past month or so.
content:
Hackers breached the U.S. Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, Cloud One, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in an intrusion discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system.

Reuters reported the breach on Nov. 27, 2026. The discovery caused disruption across the platform, according to the report. Reuters could not establish who the hackers were, the full scope of the intrusion, or whether any data was stolen.

One source told Reuters that the intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane of the system. Efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One have been paused. U.S. Cyber Command was brought in to assess the breach, according to follow-up reporting. The Air Force declined to comment on specifics.

What Cloud One does

Cloud One, started in 2017, combines computing resources from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet to power scores of applications, including personnel data and pay, logistics and maintenance.

That breadth is what makes the breach significant: the platform does not run a single program, but many of the back-office systems the Air Force relies on every day.

What it means here

There is no confirmed report that any local person's data was affected. That point matters, and it should not be lost in the scale of the story.

South Texas is home to major Air Force installations, including Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, and many local families include service members and veterans whose personnel and pay records run on systems like this one. A breach of a platform that handles personnel data and pay is therefore relevant to readers here, even though Reuters could not establish whether any data was stolen, and no local impact has been confirmed.

What is known so far is limited to what Reuters reported: a breach, discovered during upgrade work within the past month or so, that disrupted the platform and paused migration work. Who did it, how far they got, and what, if anything, they took remain unestablished.
